articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites the community to a discussion on February 8 at 4 p.m. for a compelling talk by Dr. Rupa Basu. A free livestreamed Zoom and YouTube event titled “Health Impacts from Heat: What to Know and What You Can Do,” Basu will discuss the known negative healthcare impacts of climate pollution. She will also discuss achievable, current solutions for reducing and avoiding heat-related health risks. Dr. Basu identifies heat increases and their resulting health impacts as a global problem. Heat deaths are reported worldwide and are currently significantly underreported. She will present the scientific consensus on the health impacts of rising temperatures, such as the known cardiovascular impacts and adverse birth and mental health outcomes, providing examples from California epidemiologic studies. Basu’s own research quantifies heat-related health disparities, primarily by race and ethnicity, and identifies reasons for these disparities. Prior to joining OEHHA, she worked at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, after obtaining her PhD in epidemiology from Johns Hopkins University and her MPH from UCLA. She serves on several national and state climate change committees and has been a frequent guest speaker in academic settings, including UC Berkeley, and for governmental leaders including California Governor Gavin Newsom. Basu was featured in the “Mercury Rising” episode of the Emmy award-winning climate change documentary, “Years of Living Dangerously.” Her work is widely cited in the new media, including the New York Times, the New Yorker, Loa Angeles Times, SF Chronicle, National Public Radio, and BBC World News. articles.text: The City of Piedmont took the first step towards implementing its updated Housing Element when it issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the development of a Moraga Canyon Specific Plan on January 23. Responses are due March 13, 2023. The city expects to select a consultant and begin the Specific Plan process in late Spring 2023. Once a consultant has been selected, the Specific Plan process is expected to take 18-24 months to complete. The final product of this process will be a detailed plan for how to maintain and improve existing city facilities, open space, and recreational amenities in the Moraga Canyon area while also: • incorporating 132 units of new housing, including 60 units designated for lower income households • improving wildfire safety • improving pedestrian, bicycle, and traffic safety The initiative will study all city-owned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. Public engagement Robust involvement from the community will be critical for a successful Specific Plan process. Firms submitting proposals to lead this project will need to provide a detailed plan for how they intend to engage community members in the process. Community members are encouraged to stay informed throughout the process by subscribing to the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan email list at bit. ly/3wySeTk. Affordable housing Once the Specific Plan process is underway, the city’s priority will be to identify a site within the plan area for the potential development of affordable housing. The City hopes to pinpoint an appropriate site by late 2023, with the intention of using Piedmont’s allocation of $2.2 million from the Alameda County Measure A1 low-interest loan program to support this development. The city would then need to identify an affordable housing developer to build the new homes. Specific Plan implementation The final Specific Plan will include how land use in this area could be reconfigured, and could include specific implementation measures, including: • standards and criteria for new development • infrastructure projects needed to support the Plan’s goals • financing measures to support the construction of new facilities and housing • an evaluation of the economic feasibility of the plan • fiscal analysis of potential revenues and expenses related to new development
articles.title: RFP issued for Moraga Canyon Specific Plan

articles.text: City staff will bring the 6th Cycle Housing Element to City Council for adoption after the conclusion of the State’s 90-day review period, which ends on February 16. Currently, the city expects that adoption will happen in late February or March 2023. The Planning Commission reviewed the proposed Housing Element at a special meeting on January 12 and unanimously voted to recommend that the City Council adopt the proposed Housing Element. Planning staff meeting with State reviewers Since the city submitted the Draft Housing Element to the State Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review on November 18, 2022, Planning staff have been in communication with Piedmont’s HCD reviewer, holding multiple meetings to discuss the City’s plan, answer questions, and provide a personal tour of the city sites listed in the sites inventory. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson provided a verbal update on the status of the Housing Element at the January 17, 2023, City Council meeting. Next steps: adoption, implementation HCD will provide written comments to city staff regarding the Draft Housing Element at the end of the 90-day review period. If reviewers determine that changes are needed, Planning staff will work with HCD to develop amendments, then bring the proposed updates to City Council for approval. After City Council adopts the Housing Element, the city will have three years to implement a substantial number of the proposed programs and regulatory changes outlined in the document. Some of this work has already begun: the City issued an RFP this week seeking a consultant to lead the preparation of a Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, one of the key elements of the city’s plan to accommodate 587 new homes by 2031. Implementation of the Housing Element involves additional environmental review, which is already underway; the city is currently preparing an Environmental Impact Report that studies the impacts of the homes and residents which could come to Piedmont once implementation is complete. More information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the Housing Element process, contact Kevin Jackson by email kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Russian scholar Anastasia Edel will be teaching a 6-week course online through Healdsburg American Association of University Women on the topic of Russia’s Invasion of neighboring Ukraine. The classes will be held on Thursdays from 10:00 to 11:45 a.m. from February 2 to March 9. Starting on the day when Russian missiles first struck cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine, Edel will tackle the key questions: Why did Russia become an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common heritage? How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call the war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And how does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? The cost for the 6-week course is $95. Online registration is available at healdsburg-ca.aauw. net or by mail to AAUW Forum, P.O. Box 1603, Healdsburg CA 95448. Be sure to provide your e-mail address. Classes will be presented online via Zoom. Once registered, each student will be emailed a Zoom link before each class, which will allow them to access the live class and a recording of the live classes. In 2019 Edel gave the Healdsburg audience a fascinating and well received lecture on Russian politics, history and culture. Her course will also examine the heroism of the Ukrainian resistance. Writer and social historian Anastasia Edel will lead a 6-week online class on Russia’s War on Ukraine through the Healdsburg American Association of University Women, starting February 2. Audience members will be given a brief overview of Russian-Ukrainian history to help understand why Ukraine’s rebirth is matched by Russia’s civilizational and moral collapse. The origins of Russian fascism will be explored. We will consider how the dark side of Russian culture (chauvinism, cruelty, conformism) masks and justifies the suffering in Ukraine. Anastasia will select works of Russian art that present this “dark side” and will discuss and consider whether they still belong in the world’s cultural canon. Anastasia Edel A Piedmont resident, Edel is an acclaimed Russian-American writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture. Her prose is forthcoming in the Cream City Review and World Literature Today. Since the invasion of Ukraine, she has been a frequent guest commentator on national networks, including CNN and NBC News. Of mixed Russian and Ukrainian heritage, she grew up in a small town in the south of Russia near the Ukrainian border. During the last years of the Soviet Union, she graduated with a degree in English and German studies from Kubansky State University and worked as a translator in Austria. After receiving the Chevening Award, she moved to England for postgraduate studies, and then to the U.S, where she earned her MFA in writing from Pacific University. She is on the Literary Council of the Oakland Book Festival and teaches Russian Culture and history for UC Berkeley Osher Livelong Learning Institute. Her prose has appeared in the New York Times, The New York Review of Books, Foreign Policy, Project Syndicate, and World Literature Today. To read some of her articles go to: https://www. nybooks.com/contributors/anastasia-edel/ The course uses a multimedia format, where the latest political, economic, and cultural events are illustrated with movie clips, music, art, and literature.

articles.text: Staff photo If the option of Zoom public comment is discontinued, the only way to comment in real time to school board meetings will be to be in attendance at City Hall. In the January 25 Piedmont School Board meeting, the board announced it will continue to offer remote coverage for the public via Zoom during the public comment portion of the meetings through February. There is only one regularly scheduled meeting scheduled for February, on the 8th. The school district has said it is working on finding a staff member to run the Zoom portion for the March meeting and beyond. “Right now we have lined someone up for February, but we are still working on what we will be doing in terms of staffing for public comments over Zoom for March and beyond,” said Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen. Anderson Thigpen initially announced on January 11 that Zoom coverage would be phased out, because the PUSD staff person running Zoom for the meeting is unable to continue. “Since we made that announcement we’ve heard from a number of people that have let us know that they would like us to reconsider,” said Anderson Thigpen. “I want [everyone] to knows the board is working to keep this option available,” she added. Former school board candidate Hari Titan called into the meeting via Zoom on behalf of the parent group “Parents for Educational Excellence in Piedmont,” to advocate for the option of contributing to meetings remotely. “We support the continued use of Zoom for school board meetings. We feel that public input and questions have increased transparency and improved decision making in many meetings since 2020,” Titan said. Titan also requested the school board make an agenda item for this topic whenever a solution is found to fund the continued use of Zoom. “Just know that when the board returned to in-person meetings in the fall of 2021, we felt very strongly that people should still have the option to participate in [public] comment. There are other districts that, when they returned in-person, there was no more public comment via Zoom, but we have maintained that until this staffing issue,” explained Anderson Thigpen.
articles.title: School Board continues Zoom coverage of meetings through Feb.

articles.text: The magical experience of talking to grown-ups No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling amazed when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world – from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up, the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share. But that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good. It left her awed and she wanted to know how you felt while working on it These adults made us feel like we were more than ‘just a kid’. Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. How do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising and coming from a camp director, I recommend sending them to camp. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kidsat-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen and heard. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Affirmed. Interesting. Valuable. Creative. Loved. Special. Whatever wonderful feeling was felt, it was felt because someone took the time to help them feel the goodness that was already in themself. At Camp Augusta, we believe there is something awesome in every child, we need only to take the time to notice. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and program philosophies can be found at www.campaugusta.org. articles.text: Highlanders bury last year’s champs, San Leandro, 70-28. With three games left in the regular league season, Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team is on the final leg to capture its first Western Alameda County Conference championship in the league’s 11 year history. This past week on Wednesday, January 25, the Highlanders defeated last year’s WACC winners, San Leandro, by a one-sided score of 70-28 at Binks Rawlings Gym. “Overall, we like the effort day-in and day-out. Now it’s just a matter of staying focused and staying humble,” explained PHS coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re trying to make sure everyone is on the same page offensively and defensively. We want to execute well, make sure our rotations are on point defensively, and talking a little more on the floor.” The Highlanders are set to close out their regular season with three home games in the next nine days. They’ll face Alameda on February 2, Bishop O’Dowd on February 7, and a season-finale with Berkeley on February 10. If all goes well, Piedmont will win its first WACC banner. Piedmont has defeated all three schools, a 7-point squeaker, 69-62, over O’Dowd on January 18, and two lopsided wins, 73-14 over Alameda on January 12, and 57-20 over Berkeley on January 20. Natalia Martinez scored 14 points against the Pirates. Staff Photos Eva Levingston led Piedmont with 15 points against San Leandro. O’Dowd has won nine of the last 10 WACC titles. “Closing out the season strong is definitely our focus. We want to make sure our energy and effort is channeled in the right direction. We have a lot to clean up but things are obviously going well too. We’re just trying to stay sharp. We’ve talked about not peaking too early, and now is the time,” said Gardere. Game Recap It was never a close game against the San Leandro Pirates. Piedmont led 13-4 by the end of the first quarter and 30-15 by halftime. From there, Piedmont extended the gap with 22 points in the third quarter, 52-22, and added 18 more points in the fourth and just allowed six points, 70-28. Notably, the Highlanders were still without senior forward and team captain Trinity Zamora, who suffered a leg injury against O’Dowd on January 18. Eva Levingston, Natalia Martinez, Perseas Gioukaris, and Maddie Hill picked up the scoring and rebounding load, each finishing with double-digit scoring. PHS was electric from beyond the arc, knocking down 10 three-pointers. Hill and Adrienne Blackwell each sank three baskets from beyond the arc and Martinez and Gioukaris had two each. Final scoring: Levingston had 15 points, Martinez and Gioukaris had 14 points, Hill had 13 points, Blackwell had nine points, Katarina Melian scored five. NEXT UP Piedmont (20-0 overall, 6-0 league) hosts Alameda in Binks Rawlings Gym tomorrow, Thursday, February 2 at 6:30 p.m. They will host Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 7 at 5:30 p.m. Perseas Gioukaris tied Natalia Martinez with 14 points.

Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team continues its quest for the WACC Foothill Division title with a 5-0 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Wednesday, January 25. Two days later they drew 1-1 with Alameda, also a home game. The pair of games brings their record to 6-1-4 (W-T-L), 4-1-3 in league. Although PHS has three league losses, it is still in the thick of the race. It sits in third place behind Berkeley (5-2-1, 17 points) and Castro Valley (4-4-1, 16 points). Piedmont has matches against Castro Valley this Friday, February 3, and with Berkeley on Wednesday, February 8 to determine the fate of league standings. “This league is so tight and every game is so close. Every game is like one goal apart. It’s crazy how close it is still,” noted PHS coach Dan Chubbock. “Someone is going to have to go out and win the rest of their games to win the league.” 5-0 win over San Leandro Miranda Liu scored the first of her two goals in the 12th minute of action after twice rebounding her own shot attempts in close distance. She converted a third effort after receiving a pass down the right side and running it towards goal for the shot attempt. After that, Emily Fitzgerald scored in the 25th minute on a shot from around 20 yards. She scored once again in the 38th minute after rebounding a shot on target that was saved by the Pirates’ keeper. Staff Photos Emily Fitzgerald also had two goals in a game with San Leandro. Liu scored her second goal in the 53rd minute on a through-ball by Audrey Lam. 10 minutes later, Lam scored the game’s final goal on a run down the right side and into the box. 1-1 tie with Alameda On January 27 Alameda opened the game with a goal in the second minute of action after Piedmont’s defense committed a giveaway when trying to clear the ball. It was the Hornets’ only serious threat in the game. Piedmont nearly tied the game in the 18th minute when Liu fed Lam on a nice pass on a counterattack, but Lam’s shot went straight to the keeper. Fitzgerald also had a shot go high in the 35th minute and Hailey Marshburn had a shot go wide two minutes later. In the second half, Marshburn had shots on target in the 45th and 51st minutes, but couldn’t convert. The equalizer came in Amy Derr scored on a 35-yard free kick against Alameda.

articles.text: There is no better time for viewing bodies of water than after rains. Just nine miles from Piedmont is a trail that will make you forget that you’re in the hustle and bustle of the Bay Area. It’s the Kings Canyon Loop off of Canyon Road on the way to Moraga. Parking at East Bay MUD’s Valle Vista Staging Area, the Kings Canyon Loop is a moderately challenging trail that walks alongside the Upper San Leandro Reservoir. Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is near capacity right now, providing fantastic views for the majority of the hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous view of the rolling East Bay hills. It’s a great location for birding or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat. Once you hit the 4.5-mile mark, the trail begins an elevation gain of 460 feet in a half mile, so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. But beware: at least 10 portions of the trail were saturated with mud, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. A close view of the San Leandro Reservoir is available on the Kings Canyon Loop Trail. Staff Photos The San Leandro Reservoir is at its highest level in years after the storms in December and January. A view of the reservoir from a road on the ridgeline.

At the 6-mile mark, you come to an intersection to continue on the Kings County Loop Trail to your left or to an added trail, Rimer Creek Trail to the right. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage, has opened a new, free exhibition entitled Little Island, Big Ideas. The ongoing exhibition, Portal to the Pacific, presents Treasure Island’s dynamic and unique history in a series of banners and panels on display throughout the lobby in Building One. A permanent exhibition is on view during the island’s monthly lecture series, but it is temporarily removed when events are held in the lobby. Both exhibitions are free and open to the public, Monday through Friday, from 9:00 a.m. to 5 p.m. The museum is located at 1 Avenue of the Palms on Treasure Island. Treasure Island Museum also offers several online exhibitions throughout the month. A permanent exhibition, Portal to the Pacific, is located in the lobby of the Treasure Island Museum.

articles.text: Artist and art historian Michael Stehr is resenting an illustrated lecture celebrating one of the world’s great museums. “A Stroll Through the Musée d’Orsay: An Evening with the Impressionists” will be presented at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, February 3 at 6:30 p.m. Doors open at 6:00 p.m., and admission is $20 per person at the door, Cash only. Some regard the Impressionist movement that began in Paris in the second half of the 1800’s to be the most important movement in art history since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Impressionists marked the departure from the oppressive constraints of traditional painting while serving as a stepping stone in the evolution towards becoming “modern.” The broken brush strokes and vaporous colors associated with the movement have these pictures being some of the most widely appreciated in Western art. For those cherishing the art of the Impressionists, there is one ultimate destination to enjoy these remarkable paintings: the Musée d’Orsay in Paris. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he makes a return visit to Piedmont Center for the Arts to guide visitors on a virtual stroll through this brilliant museum.
articles.title: Michael Stehr art lecture at Center for the Arts this Friday

pages.text: Wednesday, February 1, 2023 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS A fresh look at Cinderella by Disney Review by Chris Honoré If you see the title Cinderella and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative. Know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. And once again done by Disney. This is a contemporary version of what is an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here and a change there by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented Kenneth Branagh. The story, in essence, is simple and direct, and unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), relies very little on special effects or CGI. Of course, there is the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. In the main, and to its credit, this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to Lily James and Richard Madden in Disney’s latest retelling of Cinderella. construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous, English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, sadly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, and mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. And it is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the den fireplace because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the fable soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disneyesque idea of “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity, never pedantically, into the story. Ella is, indeed, courageous and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be (the last line of the film). Cinderella. articles.text: A recipe for an olive oil cake always catches my eye and piques my curiosity. I love them because they bake with a moist and tender crumb and keep for a day or so with little diminution of these ideal traits. It is still citrus season here, and by my casual observations this year is delivering bumper crops. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, February 1, 2023 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesday group visits Dracena Park By Dick Carter Spring was in the air last Wednesday, and a near record turnout for a stroll with the Walking on Wednesdays group – 50 walkers and five K-9 best friends. Charlene Louie and Priscilla Wanerus had agreed to lead the group to Dracena Park. Before the walk an announcement was made that 15 of the walkers had gone to Phil Witte’s cartoon art exhibition at the Piedmont Center for the Arts and had a great time. Charlene led the walkers on Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue and down Blair Avenue to the corner of El Cerrito Avenues where Walter Blair once had a dairy farm. This was also the edge of a quarry he created – now Dracena Park. The group entered at the bottom of the park where there is a bench in memory of Ralston Louie who died tragically in 2021. The group went up a path to the Tot Lot, where Charlene told more of the park’s history. Originally, this land was a part of the 8,000 acres that Blair bought. The property was quarried in 1852 for stone that was used to pave Oakland and Piedmont’s early streets and railways. In 1873, a quarry crew, which consisted mainly of Chinese laborers, struck water from a subterranean creek. It turned the bottom of the quarry into a lake, some 60 feet deep. Attempts to pump out the water failed, and the lake remained. It turned into a swimming hole for Piedmont boys, and sadly there were at least 12 drownings in 20 years. Finally, the quarry was fenced and locked for more than 40 years. There was a lake, called “Blair’s Pond,” complete with ducks, until at least 1977. Around 2000 the tot lot play area was renovated. Kids wanted a climbing wall and swings, while the adults wanted restrooms. Funds were raised for both, and the project was completed in 2006. Charlene then took the walkers the park’s lower entrance, and the K-9 best friends were let loose to run on the path and through the beautiful grove of redwood trees. The walkers stopped at a plaque at Storyteller Bridge, which looms above the path. Charlene also told its history. It was built in 2013 as Cole Becker’s Eagle Scout project. It replaced a bridge built in the 1920’s which crossed a ravine and creek bed. This bridge was demolished in the early 1960’s after falling into disrepair. The creek is long gone. The walkers continued up the path past huge eucalyptus trees and circled back to walk over Storyteller Bridge. At the top of the park on Dracena Avenue Priscilla Wanerus took over for Charlene and led the group on Dracena to Blair Avenue where they retraced their steps to Hillside and Magnolia Avenues and to the Exedra. The temperature started to rise and the walkers experienced something new: being warm on a Wednesday walk. At the conclusion of the walk, a little over an hour the group expressed their thanks to Charlene and Priscilla for taking them on an enjoyable tour of one of Piedmont’s most beautiful parks and sharing its history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The two small tennis courts at Beach School will be used for pickleball on a trial basis. A five-month trial for pickleball play at Beach School tennis courts will begin on February 27. The Recreation Commission will receive an update and vote to confirm or modify trial parameters at their February 15 meeting. The trial is designed to help the city evaluate options for the demand for pickleball play. During the trial period, the Beach courts will be converted to pickleball play as follows: • Court hours will be 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. (dusk) • Courts will be locked in the evenings • Organized drop-in pickleball play will be available Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.-1 p.m. • Courts will be open for informal drop-in play during remaining hours The Recreation Department will offer additional pickleball programming, including youth classes after school and free evening lessons for families and beginners. The Piedmont Pickleball Group plans to host a potluck event on March 4 to welcome new players. Meeting a growing interest Currently, kids, families and working adults have no place to play pickleball in Piedmont during the week. Pickleball is available only during limited designated hours, spread across Hampton, Beach, and the middle school courts on different days. Nets must be switched out at the beginning and end of every pickleball session. During the trial period, pickleball hours at the Hampton courts will be suspended, making 8 of Piedmont’s 10 tennis courts available full-time for tennis play. The Beach courts were selected for the trial because they are the City’s least used tennis facility, and because they cannot be used for competitive tennis play due to their small size. This trial will help the Recreation Commission and city staff better understand the full scope of pickleball demand among our community. The February to July trial period was chosen in part because it allows staff to monitor court usage across two seasons, providing a more complete picture of how dedicated pickleball courts would be used in the longterm. Community feedback will be critical in evaluating the success of the trial. The Recreation Commission invites public comments at its meetings on April 19 and June 21. The city will invite feedback through a community survey this spring, after the trial has begun.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors group recently received a tutorial from two Piedmont High AP Computer Science students. The 30-minute session at the Community Hall was the first of what hopes to be a monthly occurrence for help with cell phones and tech troubleshooting. Sophomores Ishaia Goldberg-Berman and Bruno Banuelos forfeited their lunch times to answer tech questions from the group of seniors organized by Janet Epstein. How do I get rid of all these notifications on my phone? When I delete a photo, why does my storage still say full? What is a personal hotspot? Members of the Piedmont Seniors were able to open up their phones and get answers to their questions. Topics included: cloud storage, how to change passwords, and how to connect to printers. “It’s a wonderful kind of community service and is really needed. This is starting with our Seniors Group, but I’m hoping for it to expand to more people wanting tech help and to get more tutors from the high school,” said Epstein. Participants were shown how to connect to the internet through another cell phone, a cellular hot spot turned on by Goldberg-Berman. “We are going to use her phone as the internet right now,” Epstein clarified for the group. The Piedmont Senior group meets once a month on the last Wednesday of the month. They routinely go on excursions around the Bay Area to see museums and areas of historical importance. The Tech Tutorials will be held every fourth Wednesday in the Community Hall from 12:45-1:15 p.m. More student volunteers are welcome and there is plenty of room for participants. articles.text: John Constantine — a largerthan-life personality to friends everywhere — was born in Flushing, Queens, in New York on March 10, 1951. He was the eldest child of Constantine “Gus” Constantine and Sophie Klarides Constantine, shared his name with a famous Hellblazer comic and many other Greek men, and was one of a kind. He genuinely loved people and always saw the best in them. He was a great conversationalist, networker/connector, and enjoyed talking with anyone and everyone. He could “work a room” with ease. The Constantine family moved all around the East Coast during John’s childhood, including stops in Port Washington and Smithtown in Long Island, New York as well as Great Barrington, Massachusetts. There, John made great, life-long friends and learned about business and hard work thanks to time spent in the family’s delicatessen and bowling alley/restaurant endeavors. John’s interest in business led him to Villanova University to get his degree from the Villanova School of Business, where he became a loyal Wildcat and member of both the school band — playing clarinet — and Lambda Chi Alpha fraternity. Everyone he spent time with at Villanova remained a cherished friend throughout his life. March became John’s favorite month to show his admiration and support for his alma mater — clad in blue and white to cheer on his “Cats” during basketball’s March Madness. John began his career in finance at Hertz on the East Coast. When his family moved to San Diego, he decided to also move West and continued working in finance at Warner. When Warner acquired Atari, it paved the way for the “golden days” of his career. At Atari, he helped globalize operations for the iconic video game brand while living abroad in Hong Kong and London. His time in China led him to take on roles as president of the Americas at Bondwell, General Electronics, and Elite Industrial Group and drove him to share his knowledge and expertise while on the board of the Hong Kong Association of Northern California. John fell madly in love with his wife — Debra Anne Cardella Constantine — when they were both living in San Francisco and met at a Bay Club party in 1984. They were engaged and married in 1985. Family and friends who came from near and far for their wedding now note that it was the beginning of their tradition of hosting visitors in the Bay Area. Many more memories were made as John and Debra moved to Piedmont and joined various organizations together — including Piedmont Newcomers and Neighbors and Claremont Country Club — that helped start and foster their loving community of friends. John and Debra welcomed twin girls — Alexandra Patrina Constantine and Jonna Michelle Constantine — in January 1987. John Constantine died on January 28, 2023. He was 71. John was an active cheerleader in the early extracurricular activities of “The Girls” and grew into their trusted confidant in financial, business, and life advice. John enjoyed being a fellow Wildcat with Alexandra. He was endlessly proud of his daughters’ professional and personal accomplishments — big and small. They inherited his laughter — even in life’s most challenging moments — as well as keeping in touch with friends all over the country and world. While John always had an appreciation for the finer things in life, he was deemed a “poster child” for retirement and enjoyed dedicating time to the things he already loved as well as trying out new activities. As a long-time member of the East Bay Wine Group, he also did wine tastings with the Friends of the Grape (FOG) in San Francisco. He learned new games — especially bridge and golf — that kept him challenged and social. Serving the community allowed him to spend time with wonderful friends, new and old. He held many committee positions at Claremont Country Club and as a volunteer with the Ascension Cathedral’s annual Golf Tournament and Greek Festival. John also continued his love of playing the clarinet in Urquhart Concert Band and in the Piedmont Community Band in the 4th of July Parade. He was committed to Mended Hearts — an organization that gives hope to heart disease patients, their families, and caregivers. John also continued his college-era connections in the Bay Area with the Villanova NorCal Alumni community, where he served as president for many years, as well as advising the Lambda Chi Alpha chapter at UC Berkeley. For an endlessly optimistic and easy-going guy, John encountered many difficult health issues recently that he could not overcome. He left this life on January 28, 2023, which was way too soon. John is survived by his heartbroken wife, Debra, and daughters Alexandra and Jonna. A celebration of his life will be held at a later date. The family suggests memorial donations in the name of John Constantine be made to Mended Hearts, Chapter 188, 1500 Dawson Road, Albany, GA. 31707 (https://mendedhearts.org/), or the Rheumatoid Arthritis Foundation (https:// www.rheumatoidarthritis.org/).

Charles Vosmer, one of the park’s balloonists, managed the park up to 1905 when its listing disappeared from city directories. The Blair Park land was still vacant in 1913 when the City of Piedmont, then six years old, voted to acquire land for parks. Voters approved the purchase of Dracena and Linda Parks, but not Blair Park. In 1917, new homes began to appear on the Blair Park site. Builder Guy Taylor built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue, both shingled and stucco styles. He returned in 1922 to build at least 6 more bungalows. As you drive along Moraga Avenue today, you can see the similarities that many of these homes share. Blair Park Today The early sketches show Blair Park in a grove of eucalyptus trees. Walter Blair thinned some of these trees to make paths and picnic areas. The Cable Company thinned more trees to make room for their attractions. Finally, more eucalyptus were thinned when the houses were built along MorBlair Park closed in 1905. This photo shows the bandstand (left) and the 28-foot bronze fountain (right). The balloon shaped sign is a reminder of the ascensions in the 1890s. The Oakland Tribune printed this sketch in 1967 with an article on the historic hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park. aga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. There were cascading waterfalls in Blair Park in the 1880s. The stream that ran down Moraga Canyon is now in a conduit under Moraga Avenue. The canyon was filled for decades ultimately creating Coaches Field. Throughout the years, parts of Blair Park have been sold. Mountain View Cemetery purchased the land between the middle lake and the homes on Moraga. Blair’s stone dam is still visible between the lower and middle lakes in the cemetery. In the 1920s the City of Piedmont bought the eastern portion of the park for its Corporation Yard. (A side note: During World War II Piedmont sold rock from the quarry in its Corporation Yard to Bethlehem Steel, enlarging the yard and nursery to almost its present size.) You may wonder, as I did, how all the Blair Park attractions could fit in the narrow strip of land between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery. For one thing, the lots along Moraga Avenue are very deep, up to 300 feet deep. They slope steeply from the street and are relatively level out to the cemetery land. They form a large, relatively flat area for the Bandstand, Venetian Canal, Japanese Tea House and all of Blair Park’s amusements. Fragments of the paved paths still exist in some of the backyards on Moraga. The name “Blair Park” continues to live on current maps of Piedmont. Today the City calls the land opposite Maxwelton Road, “Blair Park.” This is a portion of Walter Blair’s greater 235 acres, but the Blair Park of history was at the end of Highland Avenue. Continuing the Tradition Blair Park began as an amusement park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition has come full circle with Coaches Play Field and the William F Kennelly Skate Park. articles.text: A profound and moving interfaith gathering took place in Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church on Friday, January 27. Initiated by Amy Kelly, representing the Jewish Affinity Group of Piedmont, and enthusiastically embraced by Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted, this Shabbat (Sabbath) dinner of Jews and Christians honored International Holocaust Remembrance Day. In 2005, the United Nations General Assembly designated January 27 as a day to honor the six million Jewish victims of the Holocaust. It was the date in 1945 that the monstrous Nazi Concentration and Extermination Camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau was liberated. This joint interfaith event was a lively one, attended by more than 75 participants, consisting of approximately equal numbers of people of Jewish and Christian faith. The meal was served potluck, along with a hearty soup prepared by members of the church. The room was filled with conversations while guitarist and singer Isaac Zones provided beautiful music, playing classic songs such as Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah. The Friday meal ushering in the Jewish Day of Rest after sunset began with the lighting of the candles, a prayer beautifully chanted in Hebrew by 13-yearold Aaron Bennett. and a prayer over the braided bread known as challah. The evening was an emoPhotos by Michael Barber Amy Kelly, representing the Jewish Affinity Group of Piedmont, chats with Piedmont Community Church members Suzie Skugstad and Lisa Fuller ahead of the event. Aaron Bennett, 13, chants a prayer in Hebrew before Shabbat. Children gather around a table filled with coloring pages depicting Jewish language and culture. Singer Isaac Zones entertains guests as they line up for dinner. Dressed in a princess costume, four-year-old Olivia Castro waits with her mom, Sharon Petrowsky, for the event to begin. Ilana Bennett reads a reflection of the Holocaust written by her son, Aaron. The Piedmont Church Courtyard offers a place for children to play after dinner. Rachel Leonard shares a story revealing a Jewish tradition, naming her children after relatives who survived the Holocaust. tional one as speakers shared the pain of losing relatives and their fear that the unspeakable horrors of the Nazi Holocaust are fading with the passage of time. It was also an evening of hope as many of the Jewish participants thanked the church for making them feel “welcomed and not othered”. Among the City of Piedmont dignitaries in attendance were Mayor Jen Cavanaugh and recently elected Board of Education member Ruchi Medhekar. “This joint interfaith event demonstrates that we are stronger together,” said Cavenaugh. Sharon Petrowsky spoke about her grandmother Eva Libitzky, an Auschwitz survivor, and generously provided copies of her grandmother’s book Out on a Ledge at each table. Ilana Bennett shared a portion of her son Aaron’s Bar Mitzvah speech which was inspired by his visit to the Holocaust Remembrance Museum in Jerusalem. There he learned of a 13-year-old Czech boy also named Aaron who was killed by the Nazis in 1942. In a touching gesture, Aaron’s speech said he was sharing his Bar Mitzvah with the deceased Aaron, “a boy just like me who could not have his own Bar Mitzvah” honoring his “Bar Mitzvah twin” as a hero. “I’m pretty sure that what happened here tonight made God smile,” said Pastor Schibsted.

articles.text: and Chinese, to name a few. Beach parent Anna Kneitel even made zongzi from scratch, which is hard to make. Zongzi is a traditional Chinese rice dish made of glutinous rice stuffed with different fillings and wrapped with bamboo leaves. Anna looked up the recipe and went to the grocery store to buy the ingredients just for this event. Tammy Choi, another Beach parent, made Tteokbokki, a Korean spicy rice cake. People also shared oranges, dumplings, and noodles, foods that traditionally bring good luck and fortune. It was beautiful how it all came together, and we are so appreciative of the outpouring and support from the community. Bầu cua tôm cá – which translates to “Gourd, Crab, Shrimp, Fish” – is a Vietnamese game traditionally played during Tết. There are three dice and a board with six objects on them: a deer, gourd, chicken, fish, crab, and shrimp. We played with candy, and players tried to guess which animal would appear on the dice. The kids were taught to be generous if they won and gracious if they lost, as well as to give to others during the rest of the year. Guests feast at a huge spread of food. Kids enjoy the games and activities at the Lunar New Year party.
